THOUGHT: The presentation is classic for a paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia: sudden-onset rapid palpitations with prior self-terminating episodes and a very fast, regular narrow-complex tachycardia (≈190–210 bpm). Key ECG clues: short RP interval with retrograde P waves (inverted in the inferior leads and positive in V1) occurring just after the QRS, 1:1 AV conduction, and QRS alternans — all favor a reentrant tachycardia using the AV conduction system. Progressive PR prolongation immediately before termination indicates the tachycardia finally terminated when AV nodal conduction became too slow (block in the AV node) — a pattern seen with AV-dependent reentrant SVTs. The decisive finding is manifest ventricular preexcitation on the first sinus beats after termination (fusion of AV nodal and accessory-pathway conduction as adenosine effect wanes), proving an antegrade-conducting accessory pathway (Wolff–Parkinson–White physiology). Putting this together: the most likely diagnosis is orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT) using a manifest accessory pathway (WPW). Other SVTs that produce short-RP, regular, narrow-complex tachycardias are possible but are less likely given the post-termination preexcitation.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT) due to an accessory pathway — Wolff–Parkinson–White (most likely)
2. Typical (slow–fast) atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)
3. Atrial tachycardia with 1:1 ventriculoatrial conduction (less likely given retrograde P morphology and short RP)
4. Junctional tachycardia / automatic junctional rhythm (rare in adults but considered)
5. Atrial flutter with 1:1 conduction (uncommon at this rate without other ECG flutter signs but in the differential)
